interactions.label: An enzyme speeds up a reaction by shifting the equilibrium towards the products.

params.question: An enzyme speeds up a reaction by shifting the equilibrium towards the products.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Enzymes lower the activation energy but do not alter the equilibrium constant. The same ratio of products to reactants is reached — only faster. When cells need to drive an unfavourable reaction, they couple it to ATP hydrolysis instead.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Enzymes lower the activation energy, not the equilibrium position. The equilibrium constant stays the same; the enzyme simply helps the reaction reach that equilibrium faster.

interactions.label: In normal serum, LDH2 is present in higher concentration than LDH1. After myocar

params.question: In normal serum, LDH2 is present in higher concentration than LDH1. After myocardial injury, what characteristic change is observed in the LDH isoenzyme profile?

answers.text: LDH5 becomes the dominant isoenzyme in serum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LDH5 predominates in liver and skeletal muscle. A rise in LDH5 suggests hepatic or skeletal muscle injury, not myocardial damage.

answers.text: LDH1 rises above LDH2, producing the 'flipped' pattern

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Heart tissue is rich in LDH1 (H₄). After myocardial injury, LDH1 leaks into serum and exceeds LDH2, reversing the normal ratio — this is the diagnostic 'flipped' LDH pattern.

answers.text: All five LDH isoenzymes rise equally in proportion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Isoenzymes rise from their tissue of origin. A uniform rise across all five forms would not localise the injury to any single organ.

answers.text: Total LDH falls while LDH1 selectively rises

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Total LDH rises after tissue damage because enzymes leak from injured cells. A fall in total LDH alongside a selective LDH1 rise is not a recognised pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: After myocardial injury, LDH1 rises above LDH2 — the 'flipped' pattern. Heart tissue contains predominantly LDH1 (H₄), so its release reverses the normal serum LDH2 > LDH1 ratio.
Well done. The LDH1 > LDH2 'flipped' pattern is a classic indicator of myocardial injury because heart tissue is rich in the LDH1 (H₄) isoenzyme.

interactions.label: According to Koshland's induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds t

params.question: According to Koshland's induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the enzyme's active site?

answers.text: The active site remains rigid and is already perfectly complementary to the substrate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes Fischer's lock-and-key model. It explains specificity but cannot account for how binding energy is harnessed to promote catalysis.

answers.text: The active site changes shape upon substrate binding, positioning catalytic groups correctly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In the induced-fit model the active site is flexible — it changes conformation as the substrate binds, aligning catalytic residues precisely and excluding water to drive the reaction forward.

answers.text: The enzyme dissociates into its individual subunits to accommodate the substrate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subunit dissociation would destroy the active site architecture. Induced fit involves a conformational change within the intact enzyme, not disassembly.

answers.text: The substrate is converted to product without any conformational change in the enzyme

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Structural studies show that most enzymes undergo measurable conformational changes upon substrate binding. A fully rigid enzyme cannot explain how binding energy is used to promote catalysis.

overallFeedback.feedback: In Koshland's induced-fit model, the active site is flexible. It changes shape when the substrate binds, positioning catalytic groups correctly and pushing water out — this is the currently accepted model of enzyme action.
Correct. Induced fit explains both specificity and catalytic power: the flexible active site reshapes upon binding, straining the substrate towards the transition state.

interactions.label: Most human enzymes have an optimum temperature near 37°C. What primarily happens

params.question: Most human enzymes have an optimum temperature near 37°C. What primarily happens to enzyme activity when body temperature rises well above this optimum?

answers.text: Activity continues to increase because molecular collisions are faster

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although collision frequency rises with temperature, above the optimum the protein begins to unfold. Denaturation dominates, and activity drops sharply.

answers.text: Activity drops sharply because the protein unfolds and the active site loses its shape

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Above the optimum, thermal energy disrupts the weak bonds maintaining the enzyme's three-dimensional structure. The active site loses its precise shape — this is why fevers above 41°C are clinically dangerous.

answers.text: Activity remains constant because human enzymes are inherently thermostable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Human enzymes are optimised for 37°C, not thermostable at all temperatures. Even a few degrees above the optimum can cause significant loss of tertiary structure and activity.

answers.text: Activity drops because the substrate becomes unstable at higher temperatures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The rate-limiting factor is the enzyme, not the substrate. It is the protein that denatures when heated beyond its optimum, losing the precisely folded active site needed for catalysis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Above the optimum temperature, the enzyme protein unfolds (denatures) and the active site loses its three-dimensional shape, causing a sharp drop in activity. This is why fevers above 41°C are life-threatening.
Correct. Above the optimum, denaturation destroys the active site, which is why dangerously high fevers threaten enzyme function throughout the body.

interactions.label: Trypsinogen is an inactive enzyme precursor (zymogen). How is it converted to it

params.question: Trypsinogen is an inactive enzyme precursor (zymogen). How is it converted to its active form, trypsin?

answers.text: By phosphorylation under hormonal control

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phosphorylation is a reversible covalent modification used to regulate already-active enzymes. Zymogen activation requires irreversible proteolytic cleavage of the peptide chain.

answers.text: By allosteric binding of a pancreatic cofactor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Allosteric regulation modulates enzymes that are already active, switching them between more-active and less-active states. Zymogen activation is an irreversible, one-time cleavage event.

answers.text: By proteolytic cleavage of the inactive precursor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Enterokinase in the intestinal lumen cleaves trypsinogen to active trypsin. This is irreversible — if it occurs prematurely inside the pancreas, active trypsin digests pancreatic tissue, causing acute pancreatitis.

answers.text: By removal of its metal ion cofactor in the intestinal lumen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Trypsin does not depend on removal of a metal ion for activation. Zymogens are activated by proteolytic cleavage — removal of a peptide segment exposes the active site.

overallFeedback.feedback: Zymogens are activated by proteolytic cleavage, not by phosphorylation or allosteric regulation. Enterokinase cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin in the intestine; premature activation within the pancreas causes acute pancreatitis.
Correct. Zymogens like trypsinogen are activated by irreversible proteolytic cleavage, ensuring powerful digestive enzymes are only active in the intestinal lumen, not inside the pancreas.

interactions.label: Streptokinase is used as a thrombolytic but cannot be administered a second time

params.question: Streptokinase is used as a thrombolytic but cannot be administered a second time to the same patient. What is the reason for this limitation?

answers.text: It causes irreversible inhibition of plasmin after the first dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Streptokinase activates plasminogen to generate plasmin — it does not inhibit plasmin. The limitation on re-use is immunological, not pharmacological.

answers.text: It is a streptococcal protein and is antigenic, risking severe reactions on re-exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Streptokinase is derived from streptococci and provokes antibody formation. Re-administration risks anaphylaxis or neutralisation by pre-formed antibodies, making alteplase (recombinant tPA) the safer option for repeat thrombolysis.

answers.text: It permanently depletes the body's plasminogen stores

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plasminogen is continuously synthesised by the liver. Streptokinase activates circulating plasminogen but does not permanently exhaust the supply.

answers.text: It is rapidly cleared from the blood and becomes ineffective after one dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rapid clearance alone would not prevent re-use — it would simply require a fresh dose. The actual barrier is the immune response to this foreign bacterial protein.

overallFeedback.feedback: Streptokinase is a streptococcal protein with no intrinsic enzyme activity. Because it is antigenic, antibodies formed after the first dose can cause anaphylaxis or neutralise the drug on re-exposure.
Correct. Because streptokinase is a foreign bacterial protein, the immune system produces antibodies after the first exposure, making re-administration both dangerous and potentially ineffective.

interactions.label: In alcoholic liver disease, the AST:ALT ratio (De Ritis ratio) characteristicall

params.question: In alcoholic liver disease, the AST:ALT ratio (De Ritis ratio) characteristically exceeds 2. Which mechanism accounts for the disproportionately elevated AST?

answers.text: Alcohol induces excess ALT synthesis in hepatocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Alcohol does not induce ALT. In fact, ALT levels are relatively suppressed in alcoholic liver disease, partly due to vitamin B6 deficiency which affects ALT production more than AST.

answers.text: Alcohol damages mitochondria, releasing mitochondrial AST, while vitamin B6 deficiency lowers ALT more than AST

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Alcohol selectively injures mitochondria, releasing the mitochondrial isoform of AST. Additionally, chronic alcohol use depletes pyridoxal phosphate (B6), a cofactor for both transaminases, but its lack reduces ALT activity more than AST.

answers.text: Alcohol converts ALT to AST within hepatocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ALT and AST are distinct enzymes encoded by different genes. One cannot be converted to the other; the ratio changes because their release and synthesis are affected differently.

answers.text: AST is more stable than ALT in the serum of alcohol users

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serum half-lives of AST and ALT are not significantly altered by alcohol intake. The elevated ratio reflects increased mitochondrial AST release and reduced ALT production from B6 deficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: Alcohol damages mitochondria, releasing mitochondrial AST, and depletes vitamin B6, which lowers ALT more than AST. Together, these produce the characteristic AST:ALT ratio exceeding 2 in alcoholic liver disease.
Correct. The De Ritis ratio > 2 in alcoholic liver disease results from mitochondrial AST release and B6-mediated ALT suppression — a pattern that distinguishes alcoholic from viral hepatitis.

interactions.label: The fifty-five-year-old man with crushing chest pain had his first blood test se

params.question: The fifty-five-year-old man with crushing chest pain had his first blood test sent for a marker that is not an enzyme. Which marker is the gold standard for confirming myocardial injury?

answers.text: Creatine kinase–MB (CK-MB)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CK-MB is an enzyme isoenzyme useful for detecting re-infarction (it clears in 2–3 days), but the gold-standard first-line marker is troponin — a structural protein, not an enzyme.

answers.text: Cardiac troponin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cardiac troponin is a structural protein of the contractile apparatus, not an enzyme. It is the most specific marker for myocardial injury and must be repeated to show a diagnostic rise and fall over time.

answers.text: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH1)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: LDH1 is an enzyme isoenzyme. While the 'flipped' LDH pattern supports myocardial injury, troponin has replaced LDH as the gold-standard cardiac marker because of its superior tissue specificity.

answers.text: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: AST is a non-specific enzyme found in liver, heart, and skeletal muscle. It rises in myocardial infarction but lacks the tissue specificity of cardiac troponin.

overallFeedback.feedback: The gold-standard marker for myocardial injury is cardiac troponin — a structural protein of the contractile apparatus, not an enzyme. CK-MB, LDH1, and AST are all enzymes and are less specific for heart muscle damage.
Correct. Cardiac troponin is a structural protein, not an enzyme, and is the most specific marker available for myocardial injury — the reason it was the first test sent for the chest-pain patient.
